result: The study examined post-mortem brain samples and blood from 45 AD patients and 44 controls, using targeted deep sequencing of 744 samples across multiple cell types (PU.1+, NeuN+, DN, blood) with a BRAIN-PACT panel of 716 genes at ~1100x coverage. APOE allele frequencies were comparable to published series, and ~94% of PU.1+ nuclei corresponded to microglia.
evaluation: All reviewers accepted the study design and methodology without critique. Reviewer 3 explicitly noted 'the authors used two methods to identify mosaic mutations' as a strength, and Reviewer 2 stated 'great care was taken to identify the limitations.' The cohort characterization and technical approach are treated as sound.

result: Variant calling identified 826 somatic SNVs (0.3 mut/Mb burden), with ~90% validated by ddPCR. Of these, 96 were classified as pathogenic (P-SNVs), with 95% validation rate. Most variants were cell-type specific, with only ~5% of SNVs and ~8% of P-SNVs shared between blood and brain, suggesting infiltrating myeloid cells account for ~5% of microglia somatic diversity.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted 'extensive molecular and functional validation of mutation candidates' as a strength. Reviewer 2 stated 'the over-activation of the cells in vitro is convincing.' The validation rates and cell-type specificity findings are not questioned by any reviewer.

result: Overall SNV burden was higher in blood and PU.1+ nuclei than in DN and neurons, and increased with age in proliferating cells. Interestingly, blood SNV burden was higher in controls than AD patients, consistent with inverse association between clonal hematopoiesis and AD risk. No difference in SNV burden was observed between AD and controls in brain cell types or across brain regions.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly noted 'the study supports an enrichment of P-SNVs in several genes...and nicely separates this from SNVs associated with clonal hematopoiesis in the peripheral blood.' No reviewer challenged these findings about overall SNV burden patterns.

result: Pathogenic SNV (P-SNV) burden was selectively enriched in PU.1+ samples from AD patients compared to age-matched controls (p=0.0003), independent of age effects (p=0.0215), with an odds ratio of 7 (p=0.0035). This enrichment was consistent across brain regions and specific to genes expressed in microglia. The association remained significant after adjusting for sex and age.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'the evidence supporting the conclusions is compelling' and Reviewer 3 noted 'their data strongly suggest that mosaic MAPK mutations in microglia are associated with AD.' Reviewer 3 acknowledged 'the sample size...is small, reflected in the relatively modest effect sizes and p-values' but concluded this 'weakness is partially ameliorated by the authors' extensive molecular and functional validation.'

result: Pathway analysis revealed that P-SNVs in AD microglia preferentially targeted the RTK/MAPK pathway, with pathogenic variants in 6 of 15 classical MAPK genes detected in ~25% of AD patients (p=0.0145 vs controls). Strikingly, 6 patients (13%) carried recurrent CBL RING-domain mutations, and 2 patients had RIT1 Switch II domain mutations.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 highlighted 'they identified P-SNVs in microglia of AD patients located within the ring domain of CBL' and noted 'an in depth analysis in re-occurring P-SNVs' as a strength. Reviewer 3 stated 'the authors report a striking enrichment for mutations in the gene CBL' and noted agreement between targeted sequencing and WES methods.

result: Functional validation showed that CBL RING-domain and RIT1 variants found in AD patients increased MAPK/ERK phosphorylation in multiple cell systems (HEK293T, BV2 murine microglia, MAC lines), with increased proliferation in cells expressing these variants.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'they further provide mechanistic insights how these variants result in MAPK over-activation...in HEK cells, BV2 cells, MAC cells and human microglia-like cells in vitro. The over-activation of the cells in vitro is convincing.' Reviewer 3 noted 'the authors demonstrated in several in vitro systems that many mutations they identified in MAPK genes activate MAPK signaling' as a strength.

result: iPSC-derived microglia-like cells heterozygous for CBL404C/Y showed increased ERK phosphorylation (~2-fold), slightly increased proliferation, altered morphology, and upregulation of glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, mTORC1, inflammatory signatures (TNF, IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-1β, complement), and AD-associated transcriptional signatures, demonstrating that heterozygosity for CBLC404Y is sufficient to drive a neuroinflammatory/AD phenotype.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 emphasized 'they further provide mechanistic insights how these variants result in MAPK over-activation and subsequently in a pro-inflammatory phenotype in human microglia-like cells in vitro.' Reviewer 3 noted this as a strength, stating 'the authors demonstrated in several in vitro systems' the functional consequences of mutations.

result: Single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis of patient microglia showed that samples from patients carrying MAPK variants were enriched for inflammatory, TNF, mTOR, oxidative phosphorylation, and glycolysis signatures, particularly in clusters 2 and 2B. Variant reads were detected at single-cell resolution, supporting that patient microglial clones carrying pathogenic mutations are associated with metabolic and neuroinflammatory signatures in vivo.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 stated 'the authors showed that in some human brain samples, single-cell gene expression analysis revealed that cells bearing a mosaic MAPK pathway mutation displayed dysregulated inflammatory signaling...This single-cell analysis was in agreement with their in vitro analyses.' This concordance between in vitro and patient data is treated as a strength.

result: Approximately 27% of AD patients presented with microglial clones carrying oncogenic MAPK pathway variants at allelic frequencies of 1-6% (representing 2-12% of microglia), comparable to frequencies in histiocytosis patients. These variants were predominantly absent from blood, glia, or neurons, and heterozygous expression was sufficient to drive neuroinflammatory transcriptional programs.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'the evidence supporting the conclusions is compelling, with the authors employing a multi-faceted approach to identify an enrichment of potentially pathogenic somatic mutations in Alzheimer's disease microglia.' Reviewer 2 noted 'great care was taken to identify the limitations of the possible conclusions and to make careful conclusions...they highlight that the pathway proposed to be affected may be an explanation for a subset of AD patients.'

result: The authors suggest that AD-associated neuroinflammatory microglial clones may contribute to the neurodegenerative process in patients, though they acknowledge the natural history is difficult to establish and it remains unclear whether clones are present at disease onset or selected later during disease progression.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted 'they emphasize that it is yet unclear whether this accumulation of pathological SNVs is a cause or consequence of disease progression' and stated 'some points especially regarding the clear connection of the seen somatic variants in microglia with a potential role in disease progression remain unanswered.' Reviewer 3 acknowledged 'this study cannot conclude whether microglial mosaic mutations cause AD or are an effect of AD.'

result: The findings are consistent with prior literature showing MAPK pathway enrichment in AD brain tissue, the role of MAPK variants in histiocytosis-associated neurodegeneration, mouse models demonstrating BRAFV600E causes neurodegeneration, and the established role of neuroinflammation and APOE4 in AD pathogenesis.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 noted 'MAPK has previously been implicated in AD neuroinflammation in the literature' and stated 'the authors' previous work shows that a genetic mouse model of mosaic BRAF activation in macrophages (including microglia) displays a neurodegenerative phenotype similar to AD' as important context. These contextual claims are accepted without challenge.

result: The authors note that APOE4 allele frequency was lower in patients with pathogenic variants (34%) than without (53%), though not statistically significant. Microglia variants were frequently absent from blood, consistent with local microglia maintenance rather than blood cell infiltration. The association with AD was not due to overall increased mutational load, and pathological features were equally distributed regardless of variant status.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated 'the study supports an enrichment of P-SNVs in several genes...and nicely separates this from SNVs associated with clonal hematopoiesis in the peripheral blood' and noted 'the authors further acknowledged that several age matched control patients were diagnosed with cancer...and carefully dissected the occurring SNVs.' These observations are treated as careful, appropriate analyses.

result: Background claims about somatic mosaicism, AD epidemiology, germline risk factors (APOE4, GWAS variants), prior studies on somatic variants in AD, microglia biology, and the knowledge gap regarding microglial somatic clones in neurodegeneration.
evaluation: These are introductory/background claims establishing context and rationale. Reviewer 3 explicitly validated this framing, stating 'the current state of the AD and somatic mutation fields puts this work into context' and describing the rationale as sound. No reviewer challenged these background statements.
